title: Words in a New Language
tagline: An experiment at Stanford, a duck in a cooking pot, and how ten Latin roots unlock thousands of English words.
card: The keyword method for foreign words, and ten Latin roots that make hard English words easy.
goal: you will learn the keyword method for new words, build keyword pictures for four words, and use ten Latin roots to decode and remember hard English vocabulary.

left_off.q: Name the five habits that make every tool work better.
left_off.a: Pay attention, make a picture, give it a place, keep it ordered, review it.

left_off.q: Which tool would you use for a short list you need right now?
left_off.a: A story chain or body pegs.

left_off.q: What is the sign that a method is working?
left_off.a: Nobody notices it: it has become part of how you act.

text: In the early 1970s two psychologists at Stanford University, Richard Atkinson and Michael Raugh, wanted to know whether a very old idea could help with a very modern problem: learning the words of a foreign language. They chose a hard test. Russian vocabulary, for an English speaker, is full of unfamiliar sounds, written in an unfamiliar alphabet.

They divided their students into groups. One group learned the words in the usual way, by repeating them. The other group was taught to make a picture for each word. The students did not know that the pictures were the experiment.

check.q: What did the two psychologists want to find out?
check.a: Whether making a picture for each word would help students to learn the vocabulary of a foreign language, compared with repetition.

parts.talk: How do you usually learn new words in a foreign language? Do you repeat them, write them, or something else?

text: The picture was built in two steps. First, take the foreign word, and find a word in your own language that sounds a little like it. This is the keyword. Second, make a vivid picture in which the keyword and the meaning of the foreign word are doing something together.

Here is an example from Spanish. The word pato means duck. It sounds a bit like the English word pot. So you picture a duck sitting in a cooking pot, wearing it like a hat, with steam coming out. When you see pato you think of pot, and the duck is in the picture. The meaning is there, because you built it.

check.q: What are the two steps of the keyword method?
check.a: Find a word in your own language that sounds like the foreign word; then make a picture joining it to the meaning.

parts.talk: Try it: how would you remember that the Spanish word caballo means horse?

text: The students who used the method remembered far more words than the others. The result was reported in the mid 1970s, and the method has been tested many times since. It is not magic, and it works best for words you can picture. But for the thousands of words you need to learn in any new language, it gives you a start that repetition alone does not.

English has a second trick for hard words. A great many of its long words are built from a small set of Latin roots. Learn ten roots, and a whole page of difficult vocabulary becomes readable. In this lesson you will do both: the keyword method for foreign words, and roots for English.

check.q: What was the result of the experiment?
check.a: The students who used picture keywords remembered many more words than those who only repeated them.

parts.talk: Which English words do you find hardest to remember? Are any of them long and Latin-sounding?

words.m: all the words a person knows, or the words of a language.
here: a word in your own language that sounds like a foreign word.
the part of a word that carries its basic meaning. Port means carry.
letters added to the start of a word that change its meaning. Re- in report.
to work out the meaning from its parts.
a word that sounds like another word.

source: The keyword method was tested by Richard Atkinson and Michael Raugh at Stanford in the 1970s. Retold here in our own words.

items.h: Say the foreign word aloud and listen for a sound-alike.
items.x: A word in your own language, not a perfect match: a part of the word is enough.
What the foreign word means in your language.

items.h: Join them in a vivid scene.
items.x: The keyword and the meaning act on each other: the duck wears the pot.
Cover the meaning, look at the foreign word, and see if the scene comes.

method.x: A root is the part of the word that carries the meaning. Learn the root and the word becomes readable. Prefixes (re-, trans-, con-) change the direction.

method.title: A root family as one scene
lines: A busy harbour (port). Ships transport goods across the sea. Workers import and export crates. Reporters report the news from the dock, and a small portable radio plays music.
trans-port = carry across. im-port = carry in. ex-port = carry out. re-port = carry back (news). port-able = able to be carried.
method.pic: A harbour where everything is being carried: across, in, out, back.

method.x: Say what inspect and prospect mean, using the root spec and the prefixes in- (into) and pro- (forward).

try.title: Pato: a duck
try.prompt: Pick any foreign word you want to learn, or use caballo = horse. Write its keyword and a scene that joins the keyword to the meaning.
try.model: Caballo sounds like cab-eye-yo. A horse with one huge glowing eye is driving a yellow taxi through the city, honking.
checks: I have a keyword that sounds like the foreign word.

try.title: Two more words
try.prompt: mesa = table (sounds like mess) and gato = cat. Make a scene for each.
try.model: Mesa: a table covered in a terrible mess: pasta on the ceiling, jam on the legs. Gato: a cat shouting 'I got it!' as it runs away with a fish.

try.title: Roots
try.prompt: Match each root to its meaning.

try.title: A root family scene
try.prompt: Choose the root dict (say) or ject (throw). Write three English words that contain it and make one scene that holds all three.
try.model: ject: A circus. A clown rejects a custard pie, so the clown throws it (project) into the air; a nurse injects it with a giant syringe. The words reject, project and inject are all about throwing.
checks: There are three real words with the root.
I can say what each means.

try.q: A foreign word sounds like 'bottle' and means 'dog'. What is the best scene?
opts: A dog balancing on a giant bottle, barking inside it
try.why: The keyword (bottle) and the meaning (dog) are doing something together.

try.title: Tell the words
try.prompt: Say the root, the meaning, and two words, for aud, vid and ject.

quiz.q: What is a keyword in this method?
opts: A word in your language that sounds like the foreign word
The most important word in a sentence
quiz.why: It is a sound-alike that gives you a picture.
The keyword and the meaning acting together.

quiz.q: What does 'transport' mean, from its parts?

challenge.title: Memory challenge: the ten roots
challenge.intro: Learn the ten roots in order, with their meanings. Make one scene for each, in a ten-place palace. Type each root back, one per line.
challenge.study: One place per root: a duck leading ducklings (duc), a pair of glasses looking (spec)...

look_back.q: What is the third of the five habits (attend, picture, ...)?
What does a mind map's central image do?
look_back.a: It is the main idea in the middle of the page, with branches spreading out.

look_back.q: When is a chain better than a palace?
look_back.a: For a short list you need quickly and have no place for.
Replacing a word you cannot picture with something that sounds like it or stands for it. It is the same idea as the keyword method.
